drivers.lead: Buemi and Hartley have shared the record since 2022, when both reached three in the same car, and both took a fourth in the 2023 finale
drivers.note: Before 2022 nobody had won more than two, so the record has only ever belonged to these two men — and it moved to both of them at once, because Sébastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley were sharing the #8 Toyota when it happened. The fourth came together too, with a lights-to-flag win at the 8 Hours of Bahrain on 4 November 2023. Neither run is consecutive. Buemi's four are 2014, the 2018-19 super season, 2022 and 2023, all with Toyota; Hartley's are 2015 and 2017 with Porsche's LMP1 team and then 2022 and 2023 with Toyota, which makes him the rarer case of a champion for two manufacturers. Six drivers sit on two, Ryō Hirakawa among them, and he won both of his in the same car as the record holders. That is what makes four hard: the title is shared by a crew of three, so holding the seat is not enough — both team-mates have to keep working too.

teams.lead: Toyota went outright ahead in 2023, stretched it to five in 2024, and then lost the run to Ferrari in 2025
teams.note: Five is a smaller number than Toyota's record suggests, and the reason is a rule rather than a result. For the 2018-19 and 2019-20 seasons the FIA replaced the top-class manufacturers' championship with a teams' title, because the award required at least two registered manufacturers and Toyota was the only one left in LMP1 after Audi and Porsche walked away. Toyota won both of those teams' championships and neither is counted here. Its five are 2014, then four straight from 2021 to 2024 once the Hypercar rules brought the grid back. Porsche is closest on three — 2015, 2016 and 2017, consecutive, and none since its LMP1 programme closed — and Audi has two, from the championship's first two seasons. Ferrari's 2025 title was the marque's first in the top class of world endurance racing since 1972, and the only one anyone has taken off Toyota since the Hypercar era began.
